values: Focus: pooled CRISPR amplicon analysis, noisy long reads, multi-reference workflows, and plant/polyploid use cases. “Our tool” reflects the current implementation plus Illumina support under development.
ONT long-read pooled amplicons; Illumina PE being added
ONT/noisy long reads, also NGS including Illumina
Deep amplicon sequencing; commonly short-read Illumina workflows
Our strongest distinction is not simply “supports ONT”, but ONT + pooled + high-similarity reference separation in one workflow.
CRISPRnano paper; CRISPResso2 docs; CrisprStitch paper; Hi-TOM paper
Not a primary design focus; general FASTQ/amplicon alignment framework
Not described as a core supported mode
NO / not described in original workflow
CRISPRnano is the closest comparator for noisy ONT analysis.
Adding Illumina removes a platform-coverage disadvantage while preserving the same downstream engine.
YES — window/anchor-centric logic and error-aware filtering
YES — adaptive Smith–Waterman local alignment + block consensus for ONT noise
PARTIAL — configurable quality filters and alignment, but not designed around noisy arbitrary-length ONT reads
NO / not a stated design goal
This is a major overlap with CRISPRnano, but becomes more distinctive when combined with pooled multi-reference deconvolution.
YES — barcoded high-throughput pooled NGS workflow
Do not claim pooled analysis alone as novelty; CRISPRessoPooled and Hi-TOM already cover pooled/high-throughput settings.
Not a stated core use case
PARTIAL — multiple amplicons/alleles can be supplied; ambiguous alignments can be excluded or expanded
Not a stated core use case
Not a stated core use case
Potentially the clearest niche, especially for polyploid plants with many highly similar homeologs.
Multiple FASTQ files in one run
YES — up to 96 files stated in paper
Batching alone is not novel; emphasize heterogeneous references/targets plus pooled classification and local curation.
Different reference / target per file in one run
YES — reference/target supplied per analysis; multiple files supported
YES — Batch TSV supports per-sample amplicon, sgRNA and settings
YES — multiple samples and multiple target sites
Useful workflow advantage, but not unique by itself.
NO for hosted web app; YES as locally installed command-line/Docker software
Phrase carefully: our advantage is local browser execution, not merely “local software”. CRISPRnano and CrisprStitch also process client-side.
YES — average/base quality filters, trimming, guardrails
Limited; authors note lack of raw-data QC as a limitation
QC is a useful practical advantage over CrisprStitch, but not over CRISPRnano/CRISPResso2/Hi-TOM.
NO (planned) — non-overlapping pairs can be retained using X-padding if one mate contains a valid target/window/anchor
Not clearly documented as a central paired-end strategy in original paper
YES for normal paired-end merge workflow; docs recommend ≥10 bp overlap when amplicon exceeds read length
YES — joins only if >6 bp overlap; otherwise reads are dropped
Paired-end reads are screened after mapping; original workflow is Illumina-oriented
This could be a strong technical differentiator if validated: retain informative non-overlapping pairs rather than discarding them solely because R1/R2 do not overlap.
Illumina paired-end consensus using base quality
PLANNED — when both mates validate the same target region, merge and keep higher-quality base at disagreements
Not clearly documented in the original paper
Merged by fastp/FLASh before alignment; merge reduces end errors
Quality-aware consensus is most valuable as part of the non-overlap-tolerant preprocessing design.
YES — analysis can be limited around predicted DSB
YES — global amplicon alignment plus configurable quantification window
YES — maps haplotypes to target editing region
YES — maps reads and extracts mutation information
Do not claim “CRISPResso2 has no window”; the distinction is our window/anchor-centric classification rather than global amplicon alignment followed by quantification.
Not clearly documented; ROI is described around DSB
PARTIAL — extensive quantification-window coordinates and left/right exclusion parameters, but not the same workflow/UI concept
Best framed as flexible exploratory control/usability rather than a primary novelty claim.
YES — central to pooled high-similarity classification
Not a stated multi-reference ambiguity focus
YES — ambiguous alignments are excluded by default or can be expanded across references
Important for homeolog-rich datasets where near-identical references can generate uncertain assignments.
Detailed reports/allele tables, but not the same interactive curation workflow
Supports exploratory use and manual validation of algorithmic groups.
User tool specification; competitor public documentation reviewed
Export selected/grouped original reads as FASTQ
Possible intermediate/output files exist, but direct selected-group raw FASTQ export is not the standard headline feature
Useful bridge to downstream re-analysis: users can take a biologically interesting classified group back out as raw reads.
User tool specification; competitor public documentation reviewed
YES — tested with large synthetic deletions; window can be expanded
Avoid claiming uniqueness; emphasize that long-read/window flexibility enables large-event inspection in the same pooled workflow.
CRISPRnano paper; CRISPResso2 docs; CrisprStitch paper; Hi-TOM paper
Base editing / prime editing specialised modes
General mutation tracking, not a dedicated prime-editing engine
Competitor advantage: CRISPResso2 is broader and more mature for specialised editing modalities.
YES — intended application and validation direction
YES — originally demonstrated in rice and hexaploid wheat as well as human cells
Plant-specific framing is strongest when tied to a real biological pain point: many homeologs in polyploid plants increase genotyping and assignment complexity.
Integrated local browser workflow, pooled noisy long-read classification, curation/export, flexible windows
Strong, validated ONT error handling; client-side; simple web UX
Very mature ecosystem: pooled, batch, WGS, multiple alleles, base/prime editing, extensive reporting
Fast client-side Illumina PE workflow; efficient browser implementation
High-throughput and economical plant-focused NGS workflow for many samples/targets
The paper should explicitly acknowledge these strengths rather than presenting competitors as lacking general capability.

Legend: YES = documented/current; PARTIAL = capability exists but differs materially; PLANNED = proposed/under implementation; “Not clearly documented” = do not claim absence without further source-level verification.
